segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Again, clap twice, three times backwards, we're all in the room. Good afternoon and thank you very much for your patience. Firstly to our distinguished guests, thank you very much Honourable Minister Likanda Mufalali, Minister of Youth and Sports Zambia.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: We thank you ED, YouthConnekt Africa Hub, We thank you our very own Max Gomera from UNDP South Africa. Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon and thank you so much for joining us. I'd like to say a special welcome also to our partners, our colleagues from the private sector, but most importantly to our young entrepreneurs, the very reason we are here.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: By introduction, my name is Nozi Pohlope, I am from South Africa. I am here representing the UNDP, Regional Service Centre for Africa. I work at the intersection of trade, industrial development and private sector development.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: It is an exciting time to be here and welcome again to our Ministerial Roundtable. So over the 24th and the 23rd of November, young people and experts came together and we convened young African entrepreneurs at the YouthConnekt African Export Accelerator Bootcamp. We explored markets, trade routes, export requirements and what it really takes to have access to these markets as a young African entrepreneur.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: What it really requires, but just as important, we created a space where entrepreneurs could articulate the challenges that they face and identify what needs to be changed in order for them to be able to trade across borders rather. We looked at it from a trader's lens and a young entrepreneurial trader's lens. So together we bring those experiences to this discussion.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: This is a conversation and that's why we call it a policy dialogue. So I implore you all as we engage to bring across not only ideas but solutions. We are going to look at it today as we know the AFCFTA presents an enormous opportunity to create this one African market, but what does the opportunity actually look like for a young entrepreneur trying to export across the border? What happens when an entrepreneur has a very good product, has identified a market and a willing buyer, but cannot navigate the documentation, afford to navigate the logistics, access trade finance or receive payment? So our objective today is to move beyond identifying the barriers that have been overstated, but actually focus on practical solutions.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: So we want to hear from the government, institutions, financial actors, private sector about what we can actually do differently. And importantly we want to leave this room with commitments, responsibilities and a clear pathway. So now please allow me to invite Mr. Yangwet, the Executive Director of the YouthConnekt Africa Hub to deliver the welcome remarks.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: A round of applause for him. Thank you. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: It's a pleasure to be here. Honorable Minister, again welcome to Kigali. Very happy to have you here with your delegation.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: My colleague as well from UNDP, of course, we are in this together. YouthConnekt Africa is a partnership between UNDP and YouthConnekt, so we are part of the same team. Dear young people, partners, it's a privilege again as I said.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We want to be brief just to frame the issue, the way we see it at YouthConnekt. When we think about trade, we think about the issue through the lens of jobs. This is a core focus at YouthConnekt Africa.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We are in a way haunted by the fact that I'm sure some of you are aware of these statistics. Between 12 and 15 million young Africans enter the workforce each year and only around 3 million out of 12 get a job in a formal sector. So that leaves around 9 million young Africans without a job in the formal sector each and every year.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So a sense of perspective, 9 million is roughly the population of Togo. So just to picture that, you have each and every year the equivalent of the population of Togo, young people, without a job in the formal sector. So that's a big, big, big challenge.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: And we believe that we have to fix that challenge first before we can tackle all the equally important challenges. And of course that leads us to trade and to job creation and therefore to trade. And the question is how do we best support our job creators, entrepreneurs, SMEs, which are the engine of jobs as we all know and growth across the continent.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So that's where we are coming from on this issue. And we've been working closely with our partners who are here closely and that's what we are looking, we're looking forward to the discussion. And I think you're right to emphasize that practical solutions first and foremost.

segments.speaker: Yann Gwet · Executive Director, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So thank you very much, it's a pleasure to be here again and looking forward to the discussion. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much for those remarks.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: We will now move directly into the presentation of key barriers, recommendations, and success stories and possible emerging solutions from the youth across the continent. I think the boot camp for us reminded us that export readiness is not simply about having a good product but also understanding how to export. So it is about knowing where the surrounding trade environment actually allows entrepreneurs to act on that knowledge.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Allow me to invite Ms. Anne Le Simon, the Acting Secretary General of Independent Continental Youth Advisory Council, known as ICOYACA on the AFCFTA. Please take us through these key reflections. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I'm sorry that you can't see me so well. But I hope you can hear me and I equally hope you can see the presentation on the screens in front of you.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: My name is Anne Le Simon. I am from South Africa but I am Pan-African and work for everyone. And we're so happy to be here.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Just two years ago, it doesn't feel like it's been two years, but just two years ago, we were in this very room having this very similar ministerial round table and we've come to some conclusions and recommendations that we got from young people, young entrepreneurs like yourself. So now we want to see how far have we come? What is the work that has been done? I also challenge you that YouthConnekt reports are available online. So if you are not able to go to the one in 2024, we didn't have one last year, but you can find those reports online and look at the key recommendations and then kind of see, does it look like we've done any of what we set out to do? And then second challenge to you is when it is your turn to lend your voice to this process, please lend your voice to this process.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: This is what guides the work we do and we can ensure that when we come back, we can again measure how far we've come in the process. Okay, so let's get into it. So from Kigali 2024, we're going to look at what has changed for young traders, if anything at all.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Just briefly, the commitments that were made by the ministers present, the development partners present and others, we said that we wanted a comprehensive youth in trade program. We believe that this is being delivered. Some of the people who came a couple of days earlier did attend the export accelerator boot camps that was in 2024, as well as now a couple of days ago.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So that framework is targeted at young people who apply and who want to export. We also asked for youth friendly financial services. I would say that this one is moving, but we've also done a pilot session where working together with the AFCF Secretariat, the MasterCard Foundation, Better Than Cash Alliance and Echobank, which I'll speak about in a little bit, we're able to show that payments is one of the barriers that young people who are trying to actually trade across the borders have.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And that is not a barrier that they can solve themselves. I'll come back to that in a little bit. What about youth responsive trade facilitation? We think that this is also moving.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Youth and trade charter, which I'll speak about, also talks about how can we work with our cross-border trade associations to implement the AFCFTA protocol on women and youth in trade in real time for young people. I'm going to skip to access to resources for production. This has started and I think this is one that really hits at young people the hardest.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Access to finance is a huge barrier and access to finance that is affordable is a huge barrier. And to that, we have started, but there's a lot of work which needs to be done. Our organization works for youth across the continent and we've just turned five years old.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: I don't know if many of you know, but November is Africa Youth Month, so kudos to everybody. But it is also the month that ECOECA was founded. And so to celebrate the five years, we gave away five micro grants to five entrepreneurs of $500 each.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And then we need dedicated youth trade facilitation desks. This is an ongoing conversation that I don't think we can say we have started, but it is something we're still advocating to have. Now, it's really important that we have an ecosystem that works for us and which includes you.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: First of all, the development partners. Those are AGRA, Better Than Cash Alliance, ECOBANK, MasterCard Foundation, Trademark Africa, of course UNDP. They bring funding, they bring technical depth, and they also bring convening power, which is why we are here today with our esteemed ministers.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Then you need the AFCFTA, the African Continental Free Trade Area, and the African Union who brings the government, AUC, Women, Youth, and Gender, so that we can open the doors to policy. But not just have a discussion and then we go home and we took a box. We want to be able to say we are tracking the policy design, we're tracking the policy implementation, and it works.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And then of course, very important in this ecosystem is youth in trade organizations like ECOECA. You might have also heard of the AFYBC, African Youth Business Council. You might have heard of YALDA, and of course YouthConnekt, which is why we are here.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Just quickly, we noticed that getting paid was a missing link for many of you. People have a product, people have customers, people have done the paperwork. But how do I sell to somebody in Senegal if I'm from Namibia, and how do I make sure that that person pays me the money? So here, again, remember that ecosystem of partners.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: We worked with the MasterCard Foundation, AFCFT Secretariat, Better Than Cash Alliance, Echobank, and ECOECA. Oh, my apologies. I wasn't moving the slides.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Okay, they'll come and help us out. But at Creatives Connect in Accra, Ghana, we were able to take 20 young people with their products to Ghana, and the government of Ghana allowed them to not only exhibit, but also to sell those products. But as you know, people come from different countries, you have different currencies, you might not have change for the customer if they don't have the exact amount.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And that's when Echobank lent us these POS machines so that the exhibitors can onboard onto the POS machine and be able to take payments. What was interesting was going on this trip, we had to pay for excess luggage for all of the people who brought their products. This one, right? Yes.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: We had to pay for excess luggage, but going back, because they were able through the POS machine help to sell out most of their goods, they didn't have excess luggage going back. It showed young people that their products are good quality, they are desirable once you overstep the hurdle of payments. And then we have also been working with Accra, AFCFTA Secretariat on the Youth and Trade Charter, which is for cross-border trade associations, to ensure that we're implementing the AFCFTA Women in Youth in Trade Protocol.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: One of the recommendations was that we needed to be able to track how young people are trading under the AFCFTA and under the regional economic communities. And one of the ways which we've been able to do that is through the Across Borders Beyond Barriers magazine, which was launched right here at KCC just two months ago, and you can scan the QR code to read your copy. This magazine tracks young people across five regions who have been trading, what their hurdles have been, and some of the most heartbreaking policy revelations came from this.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Young people who've been smuggling goods across the border in ECOWAS and also in the SADC region, because they thought that the paperwork is just too expensive and it's too cumbersome. And then having only to find out that there was no need for them to struggle and smuggle because you have the STRs, the Simplified Trade Regimes, but these are policies designed to help young people that they knew nothing about. And what was even more eye-opening was that actually following the Simplified Trade Regime was much, much cheaper than the smuggling they've been paying for.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So this magazine documents some of those stories. I'm going to skip ahead. We've just come from the ATDF, the Africa Trade and Development Forum, two days ago, and we had a similar ministerial round table, and I will share their recommendations.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: The most important one of these recommendations, as I finish up, is that young people are telling us that small grants are much better and give a much wider reach. So if UNDP or Mastercard Foundation says, we're going to give two grants of $10,000 each to two companies, young people are saying, instead of giving $20,000 to two companies, give 1,000 young people a small grant, which they can unlock either buying a cutting machine, or they can do their paperwork for compliance, or they can get their export registration certificate, or their rule of origin certificate. So these are some of the recommendations.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And then last, certainly not least, especially to the partners in the room, we've started documenting or wanting to document young people that are underserved. Not just the ones who are in the cities, but the ones who are underserved. Those who are in the cross border, or in the border towns, and those who are also in the rural areas.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So working with YouthConnekt Africa, the AFCFTA Secretariat, Africa Youth Business Council, Umurava, and with the Mastercard Foundation, Funguba is a project that is supposed to document their stories in real time, directly from them, so that we can tell the policymakers how they can be a part of the success story for cross-border trade. Okay, the people who are in a roundtable similar to what we are in today, these are the recommendations. Let us split the big grants into micro grants, so that more young people get to access that funding and move the needle in their business.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Export compliance paperwork is a lot, because in Africa for every single country the standard is different, the paperwork required for that compliance is different, and it's really, really expensive for women and young people to be able to access that. So you can have a great product, and you might have figured out payments, maybe through the Pan-African Payments and Settlement System, and you found a buyer. That product is not getting across unless you have the correct certification, but those certification and the related lab tests that you have to do to say the product is safe for consumption or for animals and plants costs a lot of money.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So young people are saying subsidize that first export, so that I can see that this market is something I can invest in. Instead of asking me to invest in everything in the business, including the paperwork and the lab tests, they're asking that we subsidize the first export, so that they can be able to do it for themselves. And then for young people in the creative industry, the dancers, the painters, the singers, they are the business.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: They don't register a separate business. If I'm a singer, I'm the singer. If I'm an actor, I'm the actor.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: But the way in which our laws are written is for people who registered a separate business for themselves, and therefore are not able to get the right paperwork and things like that to get across, but they also need capacity building that is exactly for their industry, which includes a lot of intellectual property protection. And then lastly, let's keep teaching on the trade tools. The people who are at the boot camp, some of you were hearing about the Africa Trade Observatory for the first time, or the e-tariff book that's been around for almost six years now, hearing about it for the first time.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And then lastly, my apologies, this is the structure that Ikeaka is recommending as a representative of young people in trade. We want youth in trade and civil society, they have the reach, the access to the young people, the trust of the young people, and the voice, working very closely with governments who own the rules, the regulation, and also the power to subsidize and make it a legal obligation to subsidize. And then, of course, our development partners who bring funding, technical depth, and convening power for meetings just like this.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So today, we want you guys to help us make this even deeper, better. What are we missing? When we are back here next year, or I believe in the next country that we'll be hosting, what are the recommendations that come from you? Thank you. Thank you very much for that presentation, Anele.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: We are now going to move into the discussion. And I would like us to keep the conversation focused on practical solutions. We heard from the experiences of young people across the continent.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: However, I think it's important for us to hear from them in person. So I will invite the youth to make their proposals and take us through their entrepreneurial journey. And what is that one challenge in the many stages of trading a good that stops them from closing that deal and making that transaction? So in no particular order, my young people, please present yourself, where you're from, and your proposal.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Over.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon, everyone.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: Thank you. My name is Tasha from Zambia. I'm a cross-border trader, and I've been doing cross-border trade for almost three years now.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: So I import salt from Namibia and Botswana, and I export maize bran to Namibia and Botswana. So I would just love to take you through just a short, brief journey of my export experience. So I start by making a transaction to the company where I'm importing from.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: That is, I'll use Namibia for now. A company in Namibia. So there are two ways in which I make the payment.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: So I can use a bank transfer, which is a bank TT, which will take me two days. Two days, or if the system is down, it will take me more days for the payment to reflect in Namibia. And I have another way, which is the black market, which is not regulated.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: So the challenge with the black market is that it's very expensive, because it's not regulated at the border, and they can just wake up any day and, you know, increase the rates, decrease the rates. But it's the most efficient way to, like, move money from Zambia to Namibia. So how do we trade when we can't exchange our own currency? So my solution, my proposal to the policymakers is, why don't we allow banks in border countries or in border towns to have the foreign currency which is near the country? Let's say if I'm trading with Namibia, why don't we allow, I'm from Zambia, why don't we allow Zanako Bank or at the Zambian border side to have the Namibian dollar so that I can walk in there and be able to exchange with a regulated authority which will give me a fair exchange rate and which will bring more profits to my business.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: Then the second point is transportation. I understand, to be honest, transportation is a very challenging cost. You'll find that if my capital is $4,000, you'll find that $2,000 goes to transport.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: The rest is shared among the other costs of the business. So I understand, and mostly the transport sector is run by the private sector, and I know they're also in business, and they have the factors to determine those prices. So my proposal is, why don't governments partner with the private sectors to enable SMEs, more especially that are entering the cross-border trade, to enable them maybe for two years where they subsidize their transportation costs, they subsidize their transportation costs so that maybe after two years then they can take it from there.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: I believe after two years you can be able to run in cross-border trade even if you are an SME. Then the third journey. So after I get to the border, after I get my goods, my goods move from Moavis Bay in Namibia which is 1,500 kilometers to Gatimambilo border.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: And when the goods get to the border, again, there is so much theft. And I think this is one of the discussions we had when we were at the e-accelerator. It is not just a Zambian thing.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: So these problems are not just Zambian things, they are African things. Everyone agrees there's so much theft at the border where, you know, sometimes like me, I import thought. So you'd find that 10 bags are missing by the time the truck will be arriving to its destination, 15 bags are missing.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: You'd find that some people will even lose, for those that carry small cargo, they'll lose their cargo at the border. So my proposal is there should be tight security at the border. And, you know, there are thieves at the border that are even known, but no one is doing anything to them and they even brag about it.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: So immediately a thief is caught at the border. They should be jailed. Yes, the cross-border traders need protection because we can't talk about trade when you're not safe.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: How do you trade when you're not safe? Even if the clearing procedure delays, I'm supposed to feel safe that my goods are safe at the border. But if they are not safe, I'll be panicking at night. I'll not even sleep.

segments.speaker: Tasha · Zambia (youth trader)
segments.text: And you find that now, if I'm not strong, I will stop.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you, Tasha. A round of applause for Tasha.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: So one thing, ladies and gentlemen, my colleague Anita has a white paper. When you have one minute left, she will raise it up as an indication that you have one minute remaining for your intervention. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: We're going to move to our next. We also have a microphone here. So if you're not seated at the table, please, the floor is also open to you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Just raise your hand and my colleague will bring it over to the next intervener.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Hello, everyone. My name is Elizabeth Katumba and I'm from Uganda.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I own a business called Country Styles that makes handbags like this one. And like everybody else mentioned, clearly the product is good, yeah? The customers are there. So when I was coming here for the summit, I carried so many of these.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Because in my mind, I'm thinking if I've cleared everything in Uganda, I have all the licenses, all the certificates that I need, because we are part of the East African community. In my mind, I'm thinking when I get to the border in Rwanda, the only thing I'm going to be paying is the taxes. Of which these are taxes that I don't know.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Because Uganda uses a different system and Rwanda uses a different system. So when I'm at the border, I'm asked different questions. Why are you taking the bags? What are they for? And clearly, I'm going to sell them.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So at that point, what I'm suggesting is that we have agents specifically allocated to exporters at the airport so that they know. And there's a harmonized checklist where you know if I put these goods into the system, they are supposed to ask me for the certification that I need. And if I have that, they already know the taxes that I'm supposed to be paying.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So that when I get to Rwanda, it's not a surprise to me. Because right now, the goods are still there. Because I didn't know how much I was going to be charged.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And even when I was being charged, the codes that are there in the system do not provide for goods that are made here. Or let's say in Africa or East Africa. So the goods that the codes that they're using are for goods that are imported.

segments.speaker: Elizabeth Katumba · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And yet we are trying to promote entrepreneurs that are making goods here in Uganda or in Rwanda or in Africa. So how do we get to the point where we are encouraging people that are making goods in Africa, but by not charging them as much as the goods that are being imported from like Europe or Asia? Thank you very much, Elizabeth. I will go over to my next entrepreneur.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Thank you so much. My name is Patience Mondoka.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And I'm from Zambia. I'm an economist by profession. And as well as a farmer.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So I've had the opportunity to in my journey as an economist, I work as a policy analyst. And I have had the privilege and opportunity to work with entrepreneurs, helping them in their journey as a policy analyst. And some of the things that I would like to bring to the table.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I know that the AFCFTA Secretariat is not present here. But I know if the governments are here, then AFCFTA is here. One of the challenges that we've had with the AFCFTA framework is that the feedback that we get from people is the complexity of the framework.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I know nowadays we call it the STRA, the simplified trade regime. But they say the simplification is not simple enough. So you see the documents that are presented or released by the government, according to entrepreneurs, they're very complex.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So many pages, by the way. And the AFCFTA currently, most of the frameworks are presented online. And then I think in the eAccelerator boot camp in the past two days that we had earlier before the summit, we had gone through the eTariff book.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: We had gone through the rules of origin and all that. But I'm just thinking, how easy is it for an ordinary person in the rural area to understand those things? I've had people in the meetings that we've had with the AFCFTA say, maybe patients, you understand them because you're an economist. You're a scholar and the like.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: But what about the average people that are trading? The actual people at the borders, they're not in those meetings. And they know nothing about it. Most people have had to say they find the SADC to be working for them more than the AFCFTA because it's simpler.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And maybe it's something that they have grown up with. So they know that every time I'm trading, whether they're educated or not, they can just attach the SADC certificate to their invoice. And it's simple like that.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: There's nothing like rules of origin. There's nothing like eTariff book. There's nothing like HHS code where they have to go and look for a code.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And in the rural areas, I don't know about people in other countries. But in Zambia, we do have rural areas. I don't know if everybody here lives in suburbs.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I don't know. But we do have rural areas with no internet. I'm a farmer.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So I've had to do business in areas where there's no internet, there's no what. So even when the government has released an amended trade policy, I might not know if I'm in the rural. So how best can the AFCFTA make this information simple and accessible for the ordinary cross border traders? Because they're the target market for them.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: It's not for the people that are studying these things. It's not for the people that are seated in the offices in the government. It's for the actual traders.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So my recommendation is that we can find ways of making the AFCFTA framework simple. We can find ways of making it offline. We can find ways of providing information or disseminating information even in local languages, not just English.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Then we can also set up, you know, practical training desks at the borders. The AFCA team or secretariat is not present physically in other countries. They're only at the head office in Ghana in Accra.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And then the rest of the world, they operate or execute through the governments. So can we have a committee, if it's representation for the youth, for the women, can we have AFCA, FTA committee representing or just a help desk, even at the border. So like she said, those that are having harassment at the border, theft, all those kind of things, let them have a place they can go to.

segments.speaker: Patience Mondoka (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: And like just having the things online, a website, because that now makes it complex for them. Thank you very much. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Any other hands in the room? Okay. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: So my name is from Zimbabwe.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: I'm into policy and governance. And on the side, I'm also into entrepreneurship. Just sharing a bit of the journey.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: My first recommendation is on documentation cost for young people and for children, because we do have child innovators as well as persons with disabilities. There was a time we wanted the fertilizer to be experimented with in Malawi. And one of the costs that was required was on export, experimental export permit.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: The cost for somebody who has been in the same business for ten years is still the same cost with somebody who hasn't produced anything but wants to test the product. I'm glad to say we have the Honorable Minister from Zambia. In Zambia, I'm kindly asking Honorable Minister that as meetings go on, this is one of the critical issues, the issue of documentation cost, especially for young people.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: Because I haven't yet any profit. I'm trying to test the product, which means this documentation cost is coming from my pocket for the work that I do elsewhere. So somehow it's a loss.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: But it being a loss, company X that has been ten years in the game is paying the same amount. Where is the issue of inclusion? Secondly is the issue of policy inconsistence. The SADAC we want, the Africa we want, Honorable Minister, must be centered on consistency in terms of our documentation.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: If a document is going to be required in Malawi, then I must not struggle to get it from my country of origin. So that consistency in terms of policies towards trade, it's something that also needs to be looked into. Because I had challenges where an export experimental permit was required, but from my country of origin, that did not exist.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: And I'm trying to do things legally. But then at the same time, small businesses are saying we can put your product under the seat and you can just bring it right there. So I'm also asking for that.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: Then lastly, I'm asking that for the binationals, I know my countries, Zimbabwe and Zambia have already started. When these discussions are happening on trade, when we are talking of inclusivity, we are kindly asking that we have voices that speak to young people, to children and to persons with disabilities. Because we are going to be the biggest entrepreneurs because of the demographic context that we have.

segments.speaker: Youth entrepreneur · Zimbabwe
segments.text: In my country, we are 66.6%. So if we are not part of those meetings, we will keep only be at the behind the seat, always asking for things, because we are not, because we are following more of a reactive approach. So thank you so much, Honorable Minister and our official. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: I just wanted to find out from the room, do we have any entrepreneurs from West Africa? I think we've heard from Zambia, Zimbabwe, maybe we check. Anyone from West Africa? Okay. Then we move on to other hands that are up in the room.

segments.speaker: Stephen · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Thank you very much. My name is Stephen Tweseje and I am from Uganda. I recognize the Honorable Minister in the room and everyone.

segments.speaker: Stephen · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: My concern is on, I'm a young entrepreneur in Uganda, specifically dealing in maize export, maize flour. I'm inquiring, there's an issue of middlemen. I understand how important middlemen are, important in trade, but they have become a distract in trade dealings.

segments.speaker: Stephen · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: In fact, they're no longer middlemen, but they are instead thieves. You know, a practical thief, he is known, but at the border, they know him, everyone knows him, everyone knows them, but no action is taken after that. So my question to you, or my inquiry, or my proposal, sorry, my proposal to the team, why don't we establish a checklist where a young entrepreneur who is trying to export my product, imagine on a high expense to export my product from to another country, go to the border with an original checklist that is certified, knowing or having access to everyone that this is a person who is certified to do middlemen work, or that intermediary procedure when you're meeting maybe the supplier or maybe the receiver on the other side of the country.

segments.speaker: Stephen · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So if we could have that system that tracks and then make it available for young people who are into entrepreneurship, to have them so that if, as we are going to do this trade, we know who is this middleman actually certified, am I dealing with the right person, or maybe if it's the buyer, is actually this person the real person I'm dealing with? So you find you're selling a product to a broker or a middleman, but he is presenting himself as the real business manager or the business owner. So that's something that we are facing as young people, and that's why we're like, what if we create that space where young people can have that checklist, that yes, I'm going to take my product, I'm just repeating this for emphasis, how do we practically have access to this? Thank you so much. We're going to move on to the gentleman over here.

segments.speaker: Moshave Bob Wilkins · AfCFTA youth country champion
segments.text: Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Moshave Bob Wilkins, and I'm the country champion of the independent continental youth advisory on the AFCFTA. I am only honoured to be in the same room with my secretary general, Madame Mania, and just to confirm, I agree with your observations and I just wanted to reaffirm a few observations that we could pay much more attention to, as I am also a fellow trader.

segments.speaker: Moshave Bob Wilkins · AfCFTA youth country champion
segments.text: I work with farmers in the coffee and hot culture sector, and we do it for export. So I understand the whole pain, I understand the whole nitty-gritties, like the saying goes, once the rubber hits the road. So I'll be talking about the observations that I imagine if we considered them, we could have a much more safe and calculated trip in this area.

segments.speaker: Moshave Bob Wilkins · AfCFTA youth country champion
segments.text: The first one being the practicality in the real export now. The issue of involving the youth in trade organisations and the civil society players, so that we can make sure that now we do more of the capacity building, we do I had a colleague talk about the blockers, I had another trader talk about what would be seamless trade, it's still complex. I think that is a task that can be best addressed by us, who are part of you, we are also in the same business, so we can always do this more of this capacity building.

segments.speaker: Moshave Bob Wilkins · AfCFTA youth country champion
segments.text: And then also an issue of completing trade. The issue of payments. We have already existing payment systems, but I would recommend that we also look at integrating more commercial banks, the mobile money operators and also the national payment switches that already exist, so that whenever one does a transaction, it does not become complete trade when they don't get the money.

segments.speaker: Moshave Bob Wilkins · AfCFTA youth country champion
segments.text: So we need to make sure we address that and address it meticulously and also the issue of reducing the cost of the transaction. Thank you so much. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Over to you.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Thank you so much. My name is Robert.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I'm from Uganda as well, but I operate across different markets, West Africa, East Africa and Southern Africa as well. I want to talk about two key issues that I believe need to be highlighted as far as trade is concerned for young people. The first one is ease of movement across our borders as a continent.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Now, before we start talking about trade and all of these exchanges, trade happens because there is relationship between people, and if we can't move easily across our own borders, how do we establish the relationships that are necessary for trade to happen in the first place? So that's a very critical issue that I think we need to address. Recommendation there, I think we already know it and we all know what needs to be done. We need to ease movements, we need to start getting rid of some of these visas, or at least just make it very easy for people to get these visas and move.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: That's an issue about travel and movements because relationships is what allows for trade to happen. Number two, most of my fellow entrepreneurs have been talking about trade in goods, tangible things. I trade in services, the intangibles, and I think trade in services presents tremendous opportunity for our continent as far as creation of employment is concerned.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I'll give an example. My company does two things. First is training young people with practical skills in the digital economy, but we don't just stop at training them.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: We then go ahead to make sure they find work where they can earn real tangible income. Now most of this work is not just limited to the borders of our countries. Most of this work is global, and today a young person with a computer, with internet, should not be limited to work in just a nearby community or village.

segments.speaker: Robert (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: They should be able to work for any company anywhere in the world, and that is something that I think we need to start paying very close attention to. We of course see this covered under the global agreement on trade and services in goods according to WTO, right? So what are we doing to ensure that we unlock the potential as far as trade in services is concerned, to unlock large amounts of jobs for our young people in the near future? Thank you very much. We'll take one last question.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Okay, thank you so much. My name is Onele. Greetings everyone.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I'm from South Africa, and I'm very happy to see my fellow people here. I am representing a company called Moritelo. It's a skincare brand, and it's just not only skincare.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: We transform indigenous plants into natural science-backed skin products. So our company connects farmers, research, manufacturing, and also retail distribution, and export is very important to us because in South Africa we not only compete amongst ourselves, but we compete with European skincare products. But before I get into my questions, I wrote them down so for the sake of time.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Many young Africans, Africa has abundant agricultural and indigenous resources, yet many of our countries continue to export raw materials. Why are we not importing, why are we not exporting finished products? Why do we keep on only selling the raw materials to other countries, and then we become buyers? And then I think the decision makers here, they need to introduce the investment to local manufacturing, value addition, and as well as commercialization of indigenous resources. And access to funding.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Most existing funding programs support startups, but manufacturing requires significant investment in equipment, and how can policymakers address this financial gap? So then we are able to also commercialize in a sustainable manner, especially within manufacturing. And someone spoke about youth participation within the trade policy. I think that is very important.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: We've been talking export in South Africa. Currently we sell our product on shelf through retailers, but it's very competitive, and that's when we tap into now selling the product into Mozambique as well as Botswana. We're still experiencing very difficulties as far as language barriers, custom registration, so many things.

segments.speaker: Onele (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: So I don't know today, I'm here just to hear what is going to be different and to go implement, and I would like to meet with my people. Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Please allow me to invite one last lady to give her intervention, and then we'll move over.
Thank you. May I please just take 10 seconds to add on what she said? Please.

10 seconds. Yes, I'm from South Africa. I think that the trade, the AFCFTA should actually introduce a milestone-based funding mechanism where capital is released progressively as youth enterprises demonstrate growth, productivity, as well as business viability, because access to finance for us African business, as well as more especially in farming, is a very major barrier, and we have to meet these international standards.
So that adjustment fund can really help us a lot. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: The last lady, and we're done.

segments.speaker: Brenda · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: Thank you so much. My name is Brenda Fancy. I'm from Uganda.

segments.speaker: Brenda · Uganda (youth entrepreneur)
segments.text: I may not be speaking something so broad, but I want us to imagine something, because of all that is being discussed in this room, I have a question in my mind, and if we would join up the mindset and you'd respond to me, people, I'll be glad. What if we have our, we discuss, because I believe many of here are leaders and upcoming leaders like me, what if Africa has a common currency? Have you ever thought of that? Because it would really make most of the questions that we have apparently as a continent so easy to address, so that's something I want us to think about, even as we're hosting COP, I would really love that to be thought of, and even in this YouthConnekt. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much. Can we give the youth another round of applause, please? Thank you for those beautiful interventions, and I think what came out largely is from the journey we're taking from in Zambia, is that transportation becomes a really huge issue. You get to the border, you have to deal with theft.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: The cost of trading in terms of the currency and the inconsistency, you know, you have to use the black market, which depends on how the person that you exchange with feels on that day, becomes one of the biggest challenges. We spoke about government and private sector partnerships to help with the subsidy of transportation and other costs that could be curbed to help the youth actually trade their goods. Unregulated black market rates, I spoke to that.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Also prioritization of African goods on these large retailers, which be of large importance to the youth. How do we also link them to the large enterprises, but also how do we incentivize the large enterprises to prioritize African products? So is there an incentive that we can get to a consensus with, with the private sector to say, if you prioritize our young entrepreneurs' goods and they become your suppliers, how can we meet at the midpoint? We also need to reach the people that are at the borders by simplifying how we communicate our trade regimes. So what are the ABCs of trade? Can we simplify the language of the trade agreements so that the people that actually use it at the borders are able to use it and trade because they are the people who are the traders? Documentation costs for young people.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Our lady from Zimbabwe spoke about the hefty costs that she has to pay. As a result, she's not even at reaching equilibrium in terms of her profits. How do we help with the documentation costs? Does this information sit in one place? Is there a reservoir that we can put this information where people can access it? Policy inconsistency and harmonization also came out strongly.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Do we have a plan in order for us to harmonize the standards in how we trade? There is an inconsistency of standards across our countries. We do have the agreement. However, I think there's a lot of work that still needs to be done in order for us to be able to have standards that are seamless across the borders.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Inclusivity. We speak of it, but we don't live it and we don't act it. I think it's a word that we throw around in order for us to have accessibility to funds.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: But do we make sure that these people are included from the inception of what we do? In the words of our organizations, leaving no one behind, we need to be more deliberate about bringing them to the table as we co-create these programs. Uganda spoke a lot about the middleman and theft. How do we cut out the middleman? But it also came out from Zambia, right? You have the agents that actually now translate into thefts because, you know, they're able to manipulate prices and take more than they are intended to do.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Uganda also asked, can we have a simplified checklist so that people know, but not only the young traders, the ecosystem players, the person at customs, the person who works on the taxation, the person at the border, what it is that they need to check and what it is that I have or need to have as a young trader. The gentleman over there spoke about the importance of trade and services. A lot of work is being done in trade and goods.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: But are we also making sure that there is mobility? Can we give accessibility to entrepreneurs that are trying to move their goods? How do we make allowances, be it for visas, in order for traders to be able to move their goods? Funding came up a lot. But I think I heard the gentleman from South Africa saying progressive funding, milestone funding mechanism. If I've made progress as a young enterprise, are you able to then subsidize me or fund me or help me unlock investments as I've proven myself in my entrepreneurial journey? I put it over to our honorable guests to help us with any reflections and feedback from the point of government, development organizations.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: In no particular order, I would like to invite Honorable Minister Lukanda from Zimbabwe, also Honorable Minister Mercy from Uganda, from Zambia. My sincerest apologies. My sincerest apologies, Honorable Minister.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: And then Honorable Minister Mercy from Uganda, our very own resident representative for South Africa, Mexico, and our lady, Anele Simon, who advocates on behalf of the youth. So, please, over to you.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you so much, Madam Moderator.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Firstly, I want to appreciate the young people that are involved in business, cross-border business, and they have been there and they continue being there despite having these barriers they are talking about. Let me say this. I think the barriers that we are experiencing in Africa, Africa has 1.6 billion people that should be able to trade amongst themselves.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: 1.5, 9, 1.6 billion. But with these barriers, I don't think we are making progress. And for the Africa continental trade, free trade areas, those who are in secretariat and those who are playing some role, I think you have a homework or you have something to do.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Much of your, much of Africa's programs are on paper and they don't seem to take off. We can only break these silos and allow for trade to take place. The lady from Zimbabwe was challenging us to say, look, the documentation is quite expensive.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: I wish that my colleagues from Zimbabwe were here so that some of the things we could do, talk and discuss amongst ourselves so that we can break these barriers for the young people to continue trading. If you look at it, when you look at some of the things that bring some of these barriers, we are not supposed to have barriers, let's say, for Sadiq Komesa. But if you look at it, you find that the tariffs that are being applied in Zimbabwe, maybe somehow they are not the ones applying in Zimbabwe.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Yet, maybe we are using the same system, Askuda Plus Plus or Askuda Wealth. And if we are using Askuda as a system that we want to use for trading, the codes should not be a limitation in any way. I should be able to punch the goods that I am exporting into Zimbabwe on the computer.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: And since maybe they are using Askuda Wealth, that should be able to give me the codes or the payments that I need. That applies to the lady, our young lady who was coming with bags. But these silos, if they continue being there, I think they will give us a lot of barriers.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: You find in Southern Africa, you have Komesa, we have Sadiq. On top of Sadiq, you have, yes, common customs, common customs area. And they are trading sometimes the other side, the other system or the other association or council, it gives their preference to the three.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: In this case, South Africa, Namibia and Botswana, they enjoy some benefits of that common customs area. And you come to the other side, Sadiq, again, you have a challenge or something would be okay if you are in Sadiq. But again, you find another, on top of that, you have Komesa.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: So I think we need to break these silos, which are actually a hindrance to the trade among young people. The young people should trade freely. But for the issues related to a security at the border, which was raised by our young lady here, I think it's a concern and we take it that we should work on it as a government.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: We had that experience before where when you are a farmer, a young farmer, bringing your crops in Lusaka, in our city, and you bring it, you'll find these middlemen, which the other young man from Uganda was talking about. We have broken those barriers because we have removed all those people who are receiving vegetables. You come with your cabbage, they'll get it and say, we are going to sell it on your behalf.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: And the farmer gets nothing at the end of it. So we have to kick out those people. And I can assure you, my young lady, that as a government in Zambia, those people that are trading at those one border stop areas, either in Katimambilo or Botswana or Zimbabwe, I think those will have to be kicked out to allow for free trade so that you can be able to make your profits.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Otherwise, Madam Moderator, I can say much more, but I can see that there is a lot of growth and fire and more energy from the young people that they would want to succeed. And what do we do if we have to shape this generational mission? We have to break these barriers that are actually a hindrance to our young people to trade. We cannot continue enjoying poverty as a tool in Africa when we can be able to kick out poverty and allow for growth, economically and otherwise.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Maybe let me end there. Thank you.

If you will allow me, Honorable Minister, how do we organize ourselves then as a youth to allow ourselves to break this barrier? We're at a point where we've stated and we've made the proposal, so maybe I think your guidance as to how do we organize ourselves so that when we come around this roundtable next year, we're able to say we have made these strides after making these proposals, please? Thank you so much, Madam Moderator.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Madam Moderator, Africa YouthConnekt Africa. I think we have homework or things to do. Let's not keep the information that when we gather here, we keep it to ourselves.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: I think let the information that is gathered by the young people and what they would want to see from various governments or from African governments, let it go to specific ministries. In this case, the youth ministry and other ministries that are actually part of the problem that should be resolved. So that should be able to help us.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: If at the end of it, what are the action points that we need to deliver to the governments? There are so many governments that have come in Rwanda, and I want to thank President Kagame for this initiative. It brings countries together, but we should not end here. The agreements, the action points that are being made here should reach the governments in writing to say these are the agreed positions for the young people to get involved or to trade, and these are the barriers that we have seen.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: So that governments can speak to each other. We cannot have a one border stop border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, and yet you still have challenges. Between Malawi and Zimbabwe, we still have challenges.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: I think those barriers can be brought down by letting governments know that we can act together, and that's the only way to go. If we have to fight poverty, it's for governments to act together. These silos should go, otherwise I don't think we'll make progress.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: I submit.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much, Honorable Minister. Over to Honorable Minister Mercy.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: Thank you so much, Moderator. Unfortunately, I got in a bit late, so I didn't get to appreciate the earlier part of this conversation. I am Dr. Mercy Lakisa, the Minister of State in charge of Youth and Children Affairs in the Republic of Uganda.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I think my comment, I'll pick it from my colleague, Minister. He talks about governments establishing platforms and easing trade for young people. But before we talk about governments, establishing a relationship, individual governments have a lot of systemic problems to deal with.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: For example, if as a country, for example, I'm not saying Uganda, but if as a country, Uganda is not able to make the environment conducive for its young people to trade, how then do you expect Uganda to cross the borders and effect something they expect from another country, and as Uganda, you are not bringing forth? So before we talk about intergovernment engagements, I would like for everyone in this room that as you go back home, sit as a country, as departments, specifically I'm a young person, so I will speak on behalf of young people. We are privileged that here we have ministers for youth from various countries, and I believe that first they are the contact persons that matter. They are the ones who take conversations to a higher level of decision making, for example, in their cabinets.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: If we are to talk about trade for young people, the market is not selective. For example, when you go to trade, whether it's in goods or in services, the market won't say, oh, she's a young trader, or he's a mature trader. No, the conditions are the same.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: So the question in this room for all of us today, and for me, what I think we can dissect further is how can we create conducive environments for our young people to compete? Because competition comes with a lot. First, when you talk, when you want to compete on a market, we are looking at quality. What does it take for a young person who is trading to actually bring quality goods or services to the market? Because I think when we all go to the market, we're looking for quality.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: Whether it's tomatoes you're buying, no one is going to buy rotten or raw tomatoes in a market. So it's the same thing here. How do we ensure that our young people are able to produce quality goods that can compete on the market? In Africa, I think the majority of us are farmers.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: Particularly in Uganda, agriculture is what feeds us. And now we're having conversations of value addition. Because sometimes, yes, you want to export, okay? But the product you want to export may not bring you as much.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: But if there is a value addition chain or line, you could be able to get products that you can export and make a fortune out of it. Now, going beyond quality, the other aspect is building the capacity of our enterprises. I think it was a lady who no, it was you, actually, when you were giving a wrap up.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: We talked about bigger enterprises being able to support the younger enterprises to grow. But you see, we can't talk about expanding SMEs to bigger enterprises, especially if the capacity of the young people in the different lines of production is not built. So what is your country? I would also ask myself, what's my country doing to ensure that we build the capacity of these young people? In that you look at what are the incentives that you have for these young people.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: That includes access to financing. Everything around capacity in trade is around financing. So what policies are in place in your particular countries to ensure that young people have access to financing? And with good rates, okay? I think as a country, Uganda, we are not so badly off.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: We are trying. Yes, we're trying. Because then we'll have to first start treating a young person as a young person.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: You're from school two years post-graduation. And yes, I can't compete with you, who's been on the market for 10 years. I don't even have collaterals if I wanted to go to a bank to get a loan to expand.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: So then the question would be, what are we doing as individual countries to ensure that our young people can have access to financing that can kick them off I think for me, if we could come up with practical solutions for our young people to grow in that line, I would say that Africa is finally speaking one language. I thank you. Thank you very much, Honorable Minister.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I'll move over to RR Max, please.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Thank you very much, Madam Moderator. And thank you, Honorable Ministers.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: I don't know about you, Honorable Ministers, but I'm buying popcorn because young Africans have entered the chat. And I love it. And it's good to see my Mzansi people making these interventions.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: South Africa, we've been dying to get South Africa on this stage. And when South Africa comes and the rest of the continent moves with it, I think that will do some amazing things globally. I took copious amount of notes from what you've been saying.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And I want to be sure that I answer some of these things. Because there are things, there are barriers that we have removed already. And I want to be clear that some of the things have been removed, others we're still working on.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: To run a business, this is something that you know, because you're entrepreneurs, to run a business, let me simplify it a little bit. You need a product. And that's on you as the entrepreneur.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: You need a market, somebody who will buy your product, yeah, and pay for it. Somebody who need your product and pay for it. But you also need a distribution.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: You need a way of getting your product to this person here. I'm simplifying, of course, but behind each of those three sits a whole system. And each part of that system has to work for you.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Let me give you an example. Last December, we took six South African entrepreneurs businesses to a food expo in Tokyo. By the way, as an aside, I've encouraged my staff and my colleagues not to use the term informal economy.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Because there's nothing informal about what's happening with someone who's generating revenue that sends me to school and buys bread and everything else. I call it the independent economy. Because they're just operating independent to what everybody else might be used to.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So if there's one thing we can disabuse ourselves and leave as we leave YouthConnekt, let's not call them informal. That's actually not the right term to use. Now let me give you an example.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Last December, we took six to Tokyo. One of them was Tandi Matotsi Mvalo. She makes plant-based milk powders in Cape Town.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: If you do happen to be in Cape Town, check her out. She has an audited factory and she's producing by the tons. So at the expo, she met a buyer.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Someone from a Japanese retailer with more than a thousand stores. They came back after the show. They talked price, they talked containers, they talked labels, product tick, right? Then the terms.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Full payment. One week after the goods clear customs in Japan. So she would have to make a full container, ship it, wait more than a month.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Let's see while it's going. And only then get paid. The financier said, show us the purchase order.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: She went to a bank in South Africa, said, show us the purchase order. The talks had not reached that stage. The deal did not go through.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And this is an established business. She had the product. She found the market.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: What broke was the bit in between. Getting the goods there and getting the money back. And here is some good news.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Getting paid across borders is being solved. PAPS, the Pan-African Payment System that we all know, lets African businesses pay each other in their own currencies. Who was that lady who was talking about currencies without first having to find dollars? I think that's a good first step.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: In South Africa, the South African Reserve Bank runs the system that settles payments for SADAC countries. Yours and mine included, Honorable Minister. And an instant cross-border scheme for small payments.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: It's called TCIB. It's adding banks country by country. So in SADAC, the South African Reserve Bank is doing a good job to solve this.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Now, I sat with the Reserve Bank and small businesses last month and three things struck me. The first one is moving money across currencies is hard. But the rails are being built.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So that's really good news. You have to start watching what's happening from the end of January 2027 and you'll see the progress that's being made there. Second, a payment is also a record.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Every digital sale that you take builds a history that a lender can read. That is part of the problem that you face as a young entrepreneur. People don't see you as a person.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: They see the record behind you. And the merchant records for most of some of you, not most of you, for some of you, you're totally invisible. And when they say you're invisible, they're not talking about you as a person or your color or your accent.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: That doesn't matter. The records behind what you're doing. And again, that's something that UNDP is helping with.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So as I go along, these are some of the things that we are also helping with. Because that is how a small business becomes visible. The third thing is an account on its own is not enough.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: It has to be cheap and it has to be useful. So to our trader from Zambia, I don't know where you are. The problem you described is very real, my sister.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And it is being worked on. Ask your bank when you go back if it's on PAPS. Yeah? Or on TCIB.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And keep asking. Now, payments are moving. Distribution is next.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Transport borders. Safety. The issues that we talked about.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: That is where the hard work now sits. And the question that was asked to President Kagame is a very relevant one. That moving things across Africa is a logistical nightmare, so to speak.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So where do you knock for payments? And listen to what I'm doing here. Because I'm playing a trick. This is a trick question for you.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: For payments and foreign exchange, knock on your bank. Ask if it is connected to PAPS or to TCIB. For tariffs, rules of origin and things like that, simplified trade regime, your ministries of trade should be able to help with the CFTA desk.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And the e-tariff book that is online, you can look for it. An African trade observatory that is online. For trouble at the border, yeah? Your cross-border trade.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And the trade information desk. For getting a buyer and getting one in front of you, your export promotion agency. And programs like ours at UNDP, the one that's run by that woman who's sitting across from me, could be helpful.
