segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So do this so they can harass you when you're done. When you're done. She runs a program that many of you are familiar with.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And we also run other programs in countries. And they are the go-to people. Now, you see what I've done there? I sent you to four doors.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Four places. You're busy. You're an entrepreneur.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: You're trying to develop a product. But I'm sending you to four places. That is the problem.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: You should only have to knock on one door to get this. We need a one-stop shop. One place that answers every question raised in this room today.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So you from Zambia just described it. A help desk of sorts. Offline and in local languages.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And honestly, that may be a business waiting to be built by one of you. If you're interested. A young person who knows the borders, the forms, the banks, could sell the service across the continent.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And to you, Honorable Ministers, what can UNDP do for you? Our job is to make your business attractive to everyone else. We want Zambia to be attractive to the rest of the continent. We want Uganda to be attractive, the pill of Africa.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: We want it to be attractive to the rest of the continent. To the banks, to the retailers, to everybody. We help you get certified.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So knock on UNDP. If you want to help with some getting certified, to get your records straight, that's what we do. We're building merchant record systems.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Those who are in South Africa and are familiar with how the township economy is working, look at the work that's happening there. But we're also getting you in front of buyers. That's why we take people across the continent so that Africa trades with itself.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: But also outside the continent. We do this in South Africa. Say, for example, we also have blended finance instruments.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: One in South Africa, we call it Township SPAC, that we run together with the African Bank, the Development Bank of South Africa, and the UN Capital Development Fund. Knock on our doors. If you need that, let's have a chat.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: We do this so that it can help you. Grants have a place too. Yeah? But a good grant is not about sharing money evenly.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And I do wonder, I'll just put that as a challenge, our objective should not just be to create equity. If a business needs $10,000, give it $10,000. This idea that let's split it into $500 knots, I want to challenge it.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Because the thing is, you might think you've achieved equity, but the business is still not able to move goods from Limpopo to Harare. And that is a problem. We are better off making the cake bigger than trying to break a small cake amongst a million people.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: I think that's a really challenging idea. That is what a supportive ecosystem looks like. Your product is ready.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: UNDP can help you with that.
Over to Anneliese Simon. Just two minutes.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Nosy is very strict. Just by a quick show of hands, how many of you know about the PAPS, the Pan-African Payment Settlement System? Just a quick show of hands. Okay.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Maybe we should ask how many of you are entrepreneurs or work with entrepreneurs? Not as many entrepreneurs know about PAPS. How many of you have read or know about the AFCFT protocol on women and youth in trade? Okay. The theme of this meeting is shaping the generational mission.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: My challenge is, young people, don't wait for the people from the other generations to do all the work. You as a business owner or prospective business owner, you need to be curious about the work that you want to go into. That means you need to sit online.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: A lot of these tools are existing. If you could please just go to the last slide, sir. A lot of these tools are existing, but a lot of you are not using them.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: To Tash and others, know that there's more than one trade regime that applies to you and your business. I always say it's like you're a family. I was explaining it earlier.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: In your region, you have your customs union. That's you, your mom, your dad, your sister, your brother. You're like this.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: The preferences you give each other in a customs union are the best you're ever going to get, because it's almost like the country is one country. Then you have, let's say, SACU is a customs union. Then we have SADC, where we now have our Zambians, our Tanzanians.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: They're like our cousins. We love them. We give them benefits, too, in SADC, but the bigger benefits are in the customs union, and then in SADC region.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Then we move abroad. Now we have our Ugandans, our Kenyans. Those are like our best friends, the AFCFTA.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: You have your customs union. You have your regional regime. You have then AFCFTA, and we still have benefits, but they're not going to be as great.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Then you have the rest of the world. They're not our besties, the WTO, but they're still our good friends, and we have benefits there, too. When you're looking for the best preferential treatment sometimes, yes, in your customs union, you're going to get the best you can get, and then you can start looking as the family or the circle gets bigger.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Then lastly, the AFCFTA protocol on women and youth in trade is for you. It has specific benefits, as Ms. Mercy was saying, that your government must create a conducive trade environment for you, but you guys don't even know the protocol. You don't even know that Article 10 talks about access to finance and that banks should be incentivized every time they give you finance.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: You don't know that it says business development must be made available to you, so that means you're not advocating for it because you don't know about it. Please just be curious. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much. I think today's discussion has reinforced something, that the responsibility cannot lie on the young entrepreneurs themselves, so we also need everybody in the ecosystem, governments, institutions, and the private sector that must play a part of this entire. Thank you very much for notifying me.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: So before we take any hands in the room, I would like to invite Mr. Peshant Ndizeye, Senior Programs Lead at the YouthConnekt Africa Hub, to just synthesize the key reflections and looking forward message, and then we'll open the floor to any other questions before we do the closing remarks. Thank you. So thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Again, my name is Peshant Ndizeye. I'm heading programs at YouthConnekt Africa. So the whole discussion around the barriers that we are facing, that is something that is always written in our boardrooms, because we want to be the reliable middleman between the government, the young entrepreneurs, the private sector, and development partners.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Because this discussion can't bear fruit if we don't have this table. And that is YouthConnekt. Beyond discussions, beyond what we are discussing here, YouthConnekt is aiming now to come on ground.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We are building the YouthConnekt Africa export accelerator as a program, but also a platform. Whereby we are facilitating, as Honorable Minister, you said, the capacity building. Yes.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: And then the independent traders. We are having more than 80% of them across the continent. And we want really to make sure that we put mechanisms that facilitate them to come from independent traders to the formal traders.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Because we can't have them trading beyond barriers if you are not facilitating their knowledge, as Annelle said. But also certification. In the export accelerator, we are introducing the certification of export ready.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Export ready certification. To make sure that, okay, you are doing business in your country, but how do we know that your business can succeed in Kenya or in Uganda? What are the requirements in those countries that make sure that your business can succeed in those countries? So we facilitate that journey. And when you'll be starting to you'll take a step to now go into reaching the market, you make sure, you'll be sure that my business will succeed.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So that is a process of certification. Obviously, it starts by making sure that you understand what it takes on trading, certification, the quality needed to the country. So the structure is personalized.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We have a young person. I can say that we start the journey with the person, with the business. And then making sure that all the weaknesses, all I can say the barrier that the business is facing, we make sure that we facilitate building it to be stronger by tackling all the weaknesses that the business is facing.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: That is certification. Secondly, we are building policy sandboxes. I like the fact that both honourable ministers tackled that.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: First of all is having the right policies within the country. That is the first thing. And then honourable minister, I want to assure you that the discussion here will certainly be written and be handed over to your offices.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: But also not only that. Making sure that this is discussed even in your boardrooms. Because we can have good reporters, we are having the FCFTA protocol on youth and women.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: But also we want to make them live. So we are building the policy sandboxes to have the countries now interact. We are aiming to start with six countries.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: That is I'm happy that the two even from the six I represented today. That is Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Senegal and the Gambia. We want just an experimentation.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Whereby we are certifying those young entrepreneurs. But also we go to your doors. To your offices.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Okay. We are having these young people. We are sure 100% that their businesses are relevant to your market.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: Open the door so that they can bring their product in your country. By facilitating that, we tackle all the barriers that you listed. So the rules of origin, all the tax regimes.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We say, okay, let's give it a try. We facilitate those who are certified. And then we record what are the results afterwards.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: And then from those results, we inform now how first of all to roll out. But also to build or even to strengthen the protocol that we are having. And other regional blocks, policies.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So that we have records. We have data. For which young people, if they are given opportunities, they can do wonders.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: And then I recall even the first statement that Edie made on the jobs. Because we are doing this so that young entrepreneurs can not only be facilitated, but also thank you, but also create jobs for their peers. Back home, but also even where they are going.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: We are having a lot of examples for the youth connect when moving country to countries. Let's say having your young entrepreneurs in the marketplace, having new customers. And then we have good examples that some of them are relocating even.

segments.speaker: Peshant Ndizeye · Senior Programmes Lead, YouthConnekt Africa Hub
segments.text: So this is a call to action and a commitment from the youth connect Africa that this discussion will have action after this. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much, Peshant.

segments.text: So we keep it at three. I need to ask our honorable guests if you allow us a few more moments to take the questions in the room. Thank you very much.

segments.text: Okay. So our order is one over there. Ethel, two, three, four, five.

segments.text: And then we're done. Okay. We'll start over there, and then we'll go to Ethel.

segments.text: Thank you so much. Sorry, your time is now one and a half minutes. So we can take all the questions.

segments.text: So again, my colleague Anita will rave a white paper so we can take as much questions.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: I'm going to be very short. My name is Jim.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: Sorry, one minute. The lady from ECO-Earth was the first person that raised her hand when you were speaking. Noted.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: But I think I showed the order which will go. Unfortunately, the mic is already there. It will take us time to get it there.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: So we'll go from here to there. Thank you. Okay.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: My name is Jim. I come from the Kingdom of Lesotho. I've had a lot of problems from the SMEs.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: And my suggestion is I think the rate of change or the rate of execution from the governments should be as fast as the changes that are happening in trade. I will make an example. In the past, we used to believe that the partial credit guarantee schemes is a solution for SMEs.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: But today, studies show a different perspective. We need to finance these people and let money sit there for five years. After five years, it's then that they can claim dividends.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: This is the modern day way of financing SMEs and startups. So the things we used to do and the trade agreements, the tax laws that we have, they were good in 1978. Not today.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: So my plea to the governments represented by the Minister of Trade is please execute as fast as possible so that you can enable the SMEs to be run smoothly. Because unless you do that, some of them will go to the black markets like you heard one of them say. So yeah.

segments.speaker: Jim (audience)
segments.text: And the last thing is the AFCFTA, we need to monitor its progress because its win is a solution for the SMEs we have in this room and for the whole African continent. Thank you.
Thank you very much.

Allow me to acknowledge the Minister. So I don't have much time, but maybe let me just point you to our exhibition booth, Eco Yet, because we are doing all the sort of things that you spoke about today. We are a program that seeks to help women and youth-led enterprises to access regional value chains.

And so the issues you are talking about, capacity building, you spoke about access to finance, you spoke about the ecosystem, the problems at the border, the need for an agent at the border who will help. So all the sort of issues and challenges you raised are things that we're seeking to do under Eco Yet. We are funded by the MasterCard Foundation, managed by UNDP, and we're running for five years.

But for more information, our exhibition booth is by the door. It's Eco Yet. But let me also invite you to our session tomorrow where you can hear more and also interact with some of the people who are on our project in MH1 at 11.30 where we will have permanent secretaries from six, seven countries pitching to young people to say, why should a young person live, work, and do business in your country? And so they'll be speaking about all the sorts of issues and challenges you were raising, and we'll get to hear which countries are doing better at those.
And then we hope then that they can then help each other and share practice. But we would like to have you come so that we can hear your voices as well. Thank you.

Oh, sorry. While I'm here, we do have an opportunity map as well. If you go to our booth and scan the QR code, we want to understand what are the opportunities for young people on the African continent.

So if you're offering an opportunity or if you're looking for an opportunity, are you selling something? Are you wanting to buy something? Do you have funds? Do you have good policies? Just put yourself on that map. The QR code, as I say, is there. And I've also got it here on me.
You can come and get it from me afterwards. Thank you. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: And I really appreciate being given this chance. My name is Kurupi Dathan. I'm from South Sudan.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: But basically, I represent, let me say, I'm the Secretary General for UNDP African Youth Co-Creators Council. That's the council that they have talked about. So Anela, I think, will be in discussion.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: But I just want to say that so that you guys know, UNDP is willing to work with young people. UNDP is willing to work with the government as well. That's why the Co-Creators Council was established.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: So if anyone is open to work with us or to communicate all the issues, we are the bridge between young people and UNDP. So that's something that I just want to say first. I have a recommendation and a question.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: My recommendation is, especially to you, Anela, I was thinking when you guys were talking about the issues around the border, I thought of why don't we have what we call Border Trade Police Platform. So what I mean about Border Trade Police Platform is a platform where all the traders could be able to download, and if you encounter any issue or theft at the border, you can post there. And so, and all, let me say, East Africa, Saddaq, and all that, each and every region should have their representatives within your system.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: And there, they could be able to meet with ministers every quarterly or something like that to discuss this kind of issues. And that's how we could possibly address them as soon as possible. If we say all the continent, issue.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: The second, so that's my recommendation for you. My question comes to especially the ministers. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: Some of the countries, including my country, South Sudan, they're too slow in signing into AFCTA. And this is really bringing us down, like we could not be able to cooperate across the borders. How can we make sure that this kind of countries, especially within the region, could sign in and be abide by the policies within this? So that's something that I'm trying to share with you, and maybe you guys can look into it and see what can be done in making sure.

segments.speaker: Kurupi · South Sudan (audience)
segments.text: And yes, our doors are open as the AYCC. And yeah, welcome. Thank you.
We can have our next question, please.

segments.speaker: Frank · Rwanda (audience)
segments.text: Thank you so much. My name is Frank Shimangaka, and I'm from Rwanda, and I'm proudly representing my church, which is Noble Family Church, but on the marketplace.

segments.speaker: Frank · Rwanda (audience)
segments.text: So I just wrote it for the sake of time. I hope I'm wrong, but this was a thought as I was hearing everybody sharing. And then I was wondering, how can we ensure the awareness and the understanding of the African continental free trade area are integrated into our education system in a much deeper way and more detailed way, where rather than introduced on the young people when they're emerging in the marketplace.

segments.speaker: Frank · Rwanda (audience)
segments.text: Moreover, this would equip aspiring entrepreneurs with the knowledge and the skills to understand regional trade opportunities and prepare them to participate more effectively in the African market from an early stage, where I truly understand this whole initiative of one going online and searching about it, but then how much more would it be more effective if this thing was all started from high schools, from undergraduate programs. I trust this would raise much more awareness on the matter. Thanks a lot.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: Thank you very much. My name is Ivan Otim. I come from Uganda, Kampala.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: I have spent the day yesterday really trying to listen into a lot of ideas and listening into young people making very much tremendous observations of what is not working in country. And today I'm also glad that I have my minister in-house here. My observation today on the topic that we discussed will be generalized, but one of those that I want to profoundly make is that I think we must agree that we have a knowledge management crisis as people.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: So listening into the challenges that our young people in trade are facing, if we have, for example, one-stop centers existing. I had my sister in Akyaka talking about information existing. That information is existing and in the field where I come from, that information is explicit knowledge.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: It's documented. And probably it's documented in a language that not very many young people can translate, can read. So we make so many assumptions also that when we're talking about youth, we're talking about the youth that is definitely educated, can read.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: Those assumptions is what I've kept on hearing since yesterday. So when we become realistic to the people that we are engaging, then we begin to understand that most of the things that we talk about here are not those that we definitely understand. But I also want to agree with the aspect that, let me just finish up, that private sector finance is very critical.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: So my recommendation will be for this meeting here is that if we can go back to our countries and build a framework for private sector, because so many of these private sectors run social corporate impact investment or social responsibility funds. Most of this is just thrown it out there. Most of it is actually accountability for a framework.

segments.speaker: Ivan Otim · Uganda (audience)
segments.text: So can we have a framework that then these funds can be directed to supporting targeted youth ventures? Actually, thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Thank you very much for all the questions coming from the floor. I would like to give our honourable guests just a minute, and then I have the honour of inviting Max to do the closing remarks for us.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: So a minute starting with Anele, and then we'll move over to Honourable Minister from Zambia, Honourable Minister from Uganda, and Max for our closing. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Thank you, Nozi.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: And thank you everybody for sharing so sincerely. I just want to say at IKEACA, we have a number of international trade lawyers and trade law experts like myself. We take this information, we break it down for you.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: Thank you for that suggestion. There's a solution that's been around for years now for exactly that, the NTB reporting tool, where you can report anonymously anything that happens at the border. Not only report, but you can see the reports that are coming in, and you can see the resolutions in real time.

segments.speaker: Anele Simon · Acting Secretary General, Youth Advisory Council on the AfCFTA
segments.text: So also, if you're a young person wanting to go trade at a different border, I'd recommend you look there first to see if that border is problematic and reported. But do join IKEACA. The training is free, and we make sure that it's tailored to you.
Thank you. Any closing remarks? Thank you.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you so much, Madam Moderator.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you. May I just say thank you to the youths who have been coming forth, and we can see the passion that they have in ensuring that they make it in their businesses. The issues raised, I think, let me also say that there's quite a lot that is supposed to be shared, I think, among the young people, so that that information is within reach for them, and so they are well informed in terms of advancements in some of the areas that they could be concerned with as they trade.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: Issues to do with the failure to sign up for African continental free trade areas, I think, let's push for peace in our continent, so that those areas that could be affected somehow or that are not stable, there could be peace. EOP&D is doing quite a lot in Zambia, and I think I appreciate it. Recently, I think they did something that speaks to the youths getting involved in peace and ensuring that they are champions of peace.

segments.speaker: Hon. Likando Mufalali · Minister of Youth and Sport, Zambia
segments.text: So for Sudan, we want to say let's forge those areas, and as a continent and as governments, I think we are ready to support those initiatives that will bring us together, so that the signing of some of these agreements, trade agreements that exist for Africa. Thank you so much. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: Honourable Minister Mursi. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: Once again, I would like to thank every young person in this room and friends of young people.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: It's not by age. Thank you for allowing young people to have an opportunity to discuss trade. If I'm to give my parting remarks, I think for me, I also want to agree with my brother from Sudan, Southern Sudan, and I know that here we have different regional blocks.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I belong to the ESC, Sadak is here, and as a country, I think what we have done to ensure that young people are at the centre of policy making, because at the end of the day, not just trade, everything revolves around policies, and the question then would be, what are we doing to ensure that young people are at the centre of policy making? I would like to invite all of you to accept the idea of youth parliaments. For example, in Uganda, I think we have been baptised, we have had youth parliaments, and in those youth parliaments, there are resolutions that come up from them, and they are presented to Parliament, and they have been taken up. We have had a reservation scheme for our young people to be able to participate in procurement.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I don't know about other countries, but that was a result of a platform that our young leaders were given to meet and discuss. And at the regional level, we took that also a bit higher. In August this year, September, we also had a regional East African youth parliament that had young people from the bloc, yes, from the countries, member states, and they participated in discussing issues that affect young people, and trade is just one of them.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: And because I know that the regional summits of presidents, when you talk about how do you break barriers, okay? So some of the conversations that we are having in this room today, for example, I would like to know after the discussions we have had here today, what are the steps that we are going to actually take to ensure that these conversations, the resolutions that we have had in this youth connect, I don't want to attend another youth connect where we just sit in a room and discuss, we cry about our problems, we talk about solutions, but then it's just another year, and then next year we are back here, okay? Talking about the same things. I'm not sure if I, at my age, I'm not sure if I really want to be a part of those conversations year in, year out, and we are not deliberately doing anything about them. And that speaks directly to ensuring that in your particular countries you put young people at the centre of decision making.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I am able now in Uganda to speak in cabinet to defend, because I'm a former youth leader, I'm a young person, I relate with the problems that our young people face. So for the policy makers who are in here, for my colleague ministers who are here, and all the partners, I think UNDP, I thank you for the work that you are doing, and also my colleague here talked about the support that you have been giving the young people in terms of enterprise development and ensuring that they are certified. I would like to, and I want to thank my rep, deputy rep is here, I think we have a lot of work to do now moving forward outside this room.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: But I want to thank every young person here, every entrepreneur who is in this room. It's hard to be a young entrepreneur in Africa. Personally I have tried and failed.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I hope, yes, I am not very persistent when it comes to losses. But I want to appreciate every young person in this room who takes that risk each and every single day. And back to policy, I think that's it for me.

segments.speaker: Hon. Dr. Lakisa Mercy Faith · Minister of State for Youth and Children Affairs, Uganda
segments.text: I want to encourage SADAC when we had the EAC, East African Youth Parliament, we had a representation from SADAC, and they also wanted to benchmark and also carry the same practice back home, so that when our heads of states meet to discuss and to come up with policy frameworks that can work across borders, the voices of the young people are actually captured. Beyond that, don't invite me for another YouthConnekt if we're not willing to be very intentional about solutions for young people. I thank you.

segments.speaker: Nozipho Hlophe · Moderator, UNDP
segments.text: I'd like to now hand over to Max Gomera for the closing remarks. Thank you. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Well, Minister, did you say at my age? I'm getting excited about young people being at the table. Literally. No, because I think what you need to know is that for the, I'm speaking on behalf of the young people in this room here, is that if you don't invite them to the table, I think we can actually carry away the table.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So you better have them at the table of decision making, yes. And then you'll have no table to sit. I love it.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Honorable Ministers and partners, moderator, colleagues, and all the young traders who are in this room, what a day of real work, and what a two days of excitement. Three days, actually, because I'm counting two because I was here a little bit a day into our proceedings. Dr. Matthias Naab, our Director for Africa's Regional Service Centre, sends his warm regards.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: He regrets that he was not able to join, so I'm standing for him. He asked me to close on his behalf. I'll try not to embarrass him.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And I know I'm the last thing standing between you and a dance party that's happening out there, so I'll be quick. Three things I'm taking home. And the first one is a buyer is not a payment.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Tandy, remember Tandy, who I spoke about in Tokyo, found a buyer with a thousand stores. And every exporter's dream is like that. Then the buyer said, we pay a week after the goods clear customs in Japan, after a month at sea.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: That's five weeks. She needed what most of us need when we start out. She needed somebody's uncle or somebody's aunt.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: The one who says, I believe in her, I'll carry the risk until she gets paid. Now, trade finance is that uncle or aunt. It is institutionalized, and most young Africans don't have an uncle that rich.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So, honourable ministers, our challenge is to create that trade finance that young people can reach here. It's there already, right? Fantastic. We should all move to Zambia.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So, with the banks and partners in this room as well, I don't know if there are any banks here, let's explore trade finance and learn from what Zambia has done, and a guarantee mechanism for young exporters. And let's test it on the hundred young traders from this week's boot camp. Second, certified ones trade everywhere.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Elizabeth came from Uganda, I believe. Elizabeth, where are you? No? With every license in her order, her handbags are still at the border. Our maize trader asked, is this middleman real? And is this buyer who he says he is? And our salt trader from Zambia, honourable minister, asked the question that I'll carry home with me.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: How do you trade when you are not safe? So, let's passport the young trader. It is perfectly possible, because in finance, we talk about that. We have passporting agreements in finance that enable us to use the same taxonomy and language.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: When you move from South Africa to Zimbabwe, you shouldn't have to learn a new language. We can do the same thing with trading. That the rules that you use, we should be able to use them in another country as well.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Approved at home, recognised at every door. Fees that fit a first-time exporter. Borders where goods arrive with the same number of bags they left with.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: And the good news, money is starting to move. Like the pubs that we talked about, and the Reserve Bank's own regional systems in SADC are fixing payments. And Simon's traders in Accra proved it.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Cut machines from Ecobank, and they sold out. They paid for excess luggage going there. Coming home, nobody did.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So, three measures that we need to be aware of. Simon checked the 2024 commitments in public. Today.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Some moving, some are not. That's the habit we need. So, for the export accelerator commitment framework, name the one thing that your institution will do.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: The person who owns it and the date. Next year, let's not count the speeches. And I agree with you, Honourable Minister.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Let's count the young traders who made their first sale across a border. Because that's the real show that we're being successful as YouthConnekt. UNDP will do its part through AFCFTA, through AFCFTA for youth, our supplier development programme, and the AQUAET with the Mastercard Foundation.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Visit the booth as you've been invited there. Every year, we were told by YouthConnekt director here, nine million young Africans enter the workforce with no formal job waiting for them. Most of their jobs will come from businesses like the ones in this room.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: So, this was never just a conversation about trade. We've negotiated one African market. Now, let's make it possible for an ordinary young African to earn a living in it.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Right, I don't know where the dance is actually. I made that up, did I? I declare this closed. Oh, we have some pictures.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Yes, of course. Hello. If we can all come towards the front for the group picture, and then we can let you go for the talent show.

segments.speaker: Max Gomera · UNDP Resident Representative, South Africa
segments.text: Thank you.
